summary: 18 claims on gas limits, permit-to-work testing rules, incident statistics and costs. Each was checked against a fetched page or PDF. Limits: OSHA oxygen 19.5 to 23.5 percent and 10 percent of LFL; Abu Dhabi tightens flammables to less than 5 percent LEL; H2S ladder 1, 5, 10, 20 and 100 ppm (IDLH), and smell fails at 100 to 150 ppm; CO 25 to 1200 ppm. Lives: 1,030 US confined space deaths in 2011 to 2018, 46 US H2S deaths in 2011 to 2017, NIOSH 1986: more than 60% of confined space deaths are would-be rescuers, CSB: over 60 hot work deaths on tanks since 1990. Cost: OSHA values a prevented death at $8.7 million; US hot work fires cost $292 million a year. Gulf: Abu Dhabi code, Saudi high-risk work list, IOGP Middle East 2024 (9 deaths, 28.2% of hours). Key link for the story: OSHA's permit keeps gas test results, tester and time for at least 1 year, and construction rules ask for continuous monitoring. Also verified but not counted because of the 18 claim cap: Saudi GOSI-insured worker deaths 1,009 in 2016 to 2021 (Cureus 2023, https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:37033525%20AND%20SRC:MED&resultType=core&format=json); a 2006 Doha manhole incident where five workers died one after the other (Gulf News, https://gulfnews.com/world/gulf/qatar/five-asian-workers-suffocate-to-death-in-sewage-network-manhole-1.233798); GASTAT 2024 rate of 1.1 fatal occupational injuries per 100 thousand workers. Gaps: API and NFPA 51B texts are paywalled, no Gulf gas fatality count, no Gulf cost per incident, web search budget ran out.

claims.topic: OSHA hazardous atmosphere: the oxygen band and 10 percent of the lower flammable limit
claims.figure: Oxygen below 19.5 percent or above 23.5 percent; flammable gas, vapor, or mist in excess of 10 percent of its lower flammable limit (LFL)
claims.measures: Status: stat (US federal rule text). Items (3) and (1) of the definition of 'Hazardous atmosphere' in 29 CFR 1910.146(b), for permit-required confined spaces. Cornell LII shows the same wording (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1910.146). The construction rule repeats both items in 29 CFR 1926.1202 (https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1926/1926.1202). Hot work in shipyards uses a different oxygen number: 29 CFR 1915.11 defines 'Safe for hot work' as oxygen content that 'does not exceed 22.0 percent by volume' and flammable vapors 'less than 10 percent of the lower explosive limit' (https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1915/1915.11). OSHA writes LFL in 1910.146 and LEL in 1915.11, and uses 10 percent in both. The hot work paragraphs read in 1926.352(i) and 1910.252(a)(3)(i) give no percent. They say containers must be cleaned, ventilated and tested.
claims.source_title: 1910.146 Permit-required confined spaces, paragraph (b), definition of Hazardous atmosphere
claims.publisher: US Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)
claims.quote: in excess of 10 percent of its lower flammable limit (LFL) ... oxygen concentration below 19.5 percent or above 23.5 percent
claims.use_in_story: Draw the oxygen gauge as a safe band from 19.5 to 23.5 percent and mark 10 percent of LEL as the line a worker must not cross to enter or to start hot work.

claims.topic: Abu Dhabi confined-space code: same oxygen band, but a 5 percent LEL limit
claims.figure: Oxygen between 19.5% and 23.5%; flammable gas or flammable vapour less than 5% of its Lower Explosion Limit (LEL)
claims.measures: Status: stat (Abu Dhabi regulatory text). Section 3.10(e), items (i) and (vii), precautions before confined space work. Page 10 of 14. The LEL limit is half of the OSHA 10 percent. Section 3.10(d): each permit is specific to the activity and to the time and date of entry. Section 3.5(b)(v) and (vi): the program must list equipment 'including calibration requirements' and keep a 'record of all entry into a confined space, including persons undertaking the entry and/or supervising the tasks'. The PDF came back as binary through WebFetch, so the text was read with a local extractor; open the PDF and go to section 3.10.
claims.source_title: ADOSH-SF Codes of Practice, CoP 27.0 Confined Spaces
claims.publisher: Abu Dhabi Occupational Safety and Health System Framework (ADOSH-SF), published on the adphc.gov.ae site
claims.quote: atmospheric oxygen concentration levels between 19.5% and 23.5% ... less than 5% of its Lower Explosion Limit (LEL)
claims.use_in_story: Pin Abu Dhabi on a map and slide the LEL entry line from 10 percent down to 5 percent, to show why each project needs its own limits.

claims.topic: Saudi regulation names confined spaces, hot cutting and explosive atmospheres as high-risk work
claims.figure: 26 high-risk activities in Article Nine, including 2 Working in Confined Spaces, 11 Welding and Hot Cutting Operations, 17 Working in Hazardous and Explosive Atmospheres
claims.measures: Status: stat (Saudi regulatory text). Article Nine of the Regulation on the Organization of Work in High-Risk Occupations, table on printed pages 10 to 13. The hot cutting row says 'Explosions in the presence of flammable gases in the work environment'. Article Five(7) tells employers not to assign high-risk tasks without valid permits. These are worker licences ('High-Risk Occupation Work Permit'), not a site permit to work. The annex lists 222 high-risk occupations, including Welder (114), Sewage Worker (202) and Water Tank Cleaning Worker (203). No numeric gas limit is in the text. Article Nineteen says it enters into force 180 days after Official Gazette publication; that publication was not confirmed. The PDF came back as binary through WebFetch, so the text was read with a local extractor.
claims.year: Issue year not printed in the text read (the PDF file name ends in 25)
claims.source_title: Regulation on the Organization of Work in High-Risk Occupations (English PDF)
claims.publisher: National Council for Occupational Safety and Health (NCOSH), Saudi Arabia
claims.quote: Hazard related to ventilation or internal atmosphere - including oxygen deficiency or surplus, or the presence of toxic, asphyxiating, flammable, or explosive gases
claims.use_in_story: Show a Saudi flag card that lists confined space, hot cutting and explosive atmospheres as named high-risk work, to say gas readings are part of proving a job was safe.

claims.topic: Hydrogen sulfide limits: NIOSH, OSHA, ACGIH and IDLH
claims.figure: NIOSH REL: C 10 ppm (15 mg/m3) [10-minute]; OSHA PEL: C 20 ppm 50 ppm [10-minute maximum peak]; ACGIH TLV-TWA 1 ppm and TLV-STEL 5 ppm; IDLH: 100 ppm
claims.measures: Status: stat (published limits). The NIOSH Pocket Guide page gives the REL, the OSHA PEL and the IDLH (page last reviewed 30 Oct 2019). C means ceiling. The ACGIH public page prints 'TLV-TWA, 1 ppm (1.4 mg/m3)' and 'TLV-STEL, 5 ppm (7 mg/m3)' (https://www.acgih.org/hydrogen-sulfide/). ILO/WHO card ICSC 0165, revised April 2017, prints 'TLV: 1 ppm as TWA; 5 ppm as STEL' (https://www.inchem.org/documents/icsc/icsc/eics0165.htm). OSHA's H2S hazards page also lists 'Construction 8-hour Limit: 10 ppm' and 'Shipyard 8-hour limit: 10 ppm' (https://www.osha.gov/hydrogen-sulfide/hazards). C4-gas-path.md line 136 lists the Gas page default H2S high alarm as 10 ppm and TWA as 10 ppm, equal to the NIOSH ceiling and the OSHA construction 8-hour limit; not re-checked in code.
claims.region: United States (NIOSH, OSHA, ACGIH); limits are used worldwide
claims.year: NIOSH page last reviewed 30 Oct 2019; ICSC card revised April 2017
claims.source_title: NIOSH Pocket Guide to Chemical Hazards: Hydrogen sulfide
claims.publisher: US National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH), CDC
claims.quote: C 10 ppm (15 mg/m3) [10-minute] ... C 20 ppm 50 ppm [10-minute maximum peak] ... 100 ppm

claims.figure: 100-150 ppm: loss of smell (olfactory fatigue or paralysis); 700-1000 ppm: rapid unconsciousness, knockdown, death within minutes; 1000-2000 ppm: nearly instant death

Same table: 0.01-1.5 ppm 'Odor threshold'; 100 ppm 'loss of smell after 2-15 minutes (olfactory fatigue)'. The same page lists 'NIOSH IDLH: 100 ppm', so the IDLH level and the loss-of-smell level overlap.

claims.topic: Confined-space permit: test order, recorded results, continuous monitoring and keeping the permit
claims.figure: Test first for oxygen, then combustible gases and vapors, then toxic gases and vapors; permit records test results with tester names or initials and when tested; cancelled permits kept at least 1 year
claims.measures: Status: stat (US federal rule text). 29 CFR 1910.146(d)(5)(iii) gives the test order. (c)(5)(ii)(C) also requires testing 'with a calibrated direct-reading instrument' before an employee enters. (d)(5)(i): where the space is large or part of a continuous system such as a sewer, entry conditions 'shall be continuously monitored in the areas where authorized entrants are working'. (f)(10): the permit lists the 'results of initial and periodic tests ... accompanied by the names or initials of the testers and by an indication of when the tests were performed'. (e)(6): 'retain each cancelled entry permit for at least 1 year'. Construction rule 29 CFR 1926.1204(e)(2) says 'Continuously monitor atmospheric hazards' unless continuous equipment is not commercially available or periodic monitoring is frequent enough; (e)(3) repeats the test order (https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1926/1926.1204, same text at https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1926.1204). NIOSH Alert 86-110 also says confined spaces 'should be tested prior to entry and continually monitored' (see S3-12).
claims.publisher: US Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)
claims.quote: test first for oxygen, then for combustible gases and vapors, and then for toxic gases and vapors
claims.use_in_story: Fill a permit card with three timed readings in order (oxygen, LEL, toxics) and stamp a 1 year retention tag on it, to show the permit is a record the data bank can hold.

claims.topic: Hot work fire watch after the torch is off: OSHA half hour, NFPA 51B one hour
claims.figure: OSHA: at least a half hour after welding or cutting; NFPA 51B 2019 edition: a minimum of 1 hour (section 5.6.1.1)
claims.measures: Status: stat (rule text; NFPA through its committee record, not the standard itself). OSHA 29 CFR 1910.252(a)(2)(iii)(B): 'A fire watch shall be maintained for at least a half hour after completion of welding or cutting operations' (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1910.252, same wording on osha.gov). The NFPA committee file (public inputs and committee statements dated 2020 and 2021) says the example permit text 'was not changed to reflect the code change of a minimum of 1 hour in section 5.6.1.1' and the committee wrote 'There is a recognized need for a 1 hr fire watch'. The same file records that the CSB asked for monitoring to keep gas 'less than the LFL (generally less than 10% LFL)'. The committee says it offered a First Revision while allowing 'time for further review of NFPA 326'. So the numeric gas limit was not read inside NFPA 51B itself. Also from OSHA: 1910.252(a)(2)(iv) prefers 'a written permit' for hot work; 1910.119(k)(1) says 'The employer shall issue a hot work permit' for hot work on or near a covered process (https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.119); 1926.352(i) requires containers that held toxic or flammable substances to be cleaned, ventilated and 'tested' before welding or cutting (https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1926/1926.352). The PDF came back as binary through WebFetch, so the text was read with a local extractor.
claims.year: NFPA 51B 2019 edition (committee file dated 2020 and 2021); OSHA text in force
claims.source_title: NFPA 51B public inputs and committee statements, Technical Committee on Hot Work Operations (file 51B_A2023_HWO_AAA_FD_PIResponses.pdf)
claims.quote: code change of a minimum of 1 hour in section 5.6.1.1
claims.use_in_story: Run a countdown ring after the torch goes out, 30 minutes on the OSHA ring and 60 minutes on the NFPA ring, to show how long someone must keep watching.

claims.topic: Hot work on tanks: over 60 deaths since 1990 and gas monitoring before and during the work
claims.figure: over 60 fatalities since 1990 due to explosions and fires from hot work activities on tanks
claims.measures: Status: stat. US Chemical Safety Board Safety Bulletin No. 2009-01-SB, February 2010, introduction on PDF page 2. Lesson 3 'Monitor the Atmosphere' (PDF page 3): 'Conduct effective gas monitoring in the work area using a properly calibrated combustible gas detector prior to and during hot work activities, even in areas where a flammable atmosphere is not anticipated.' The CSB web page repeats it (https://www.csb.gov/recommendations/hot-work/). Footnote 6 (page 13) quotes API RP 2009 (2002), p. 12: '(a) competent person using an appropriate combustible-gas meter should perform tests to determine flammable vapor concentrations before hot work is started.' Footnote 8 (page 13) says API RP 2009 and NFPA 51B both recommend written hot work permits. Page 11: in one refinery tank case gas was tested only at the start, 'five hours between the last gas test and the explosion', and the air warmed by 14 degrees. The bulletin gives no percent LEL number. The PDF came back as binary through WebFetch, so the text was read with a local extractor.
claims.source_title: Seven Key Lessons to Prevent Worker Deaths During Hot Work In and Around Tanks (Safety Bulletin No. 2009-01-SB)
claims.publisher: US Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board (CSB)
claims.quote: The CSB has identified over 60 fatalities since 1990 due to explosions and fires from hot work activities on tanks.
claims.use_in_story: Pair a tank icon with a 60+ counter and a gas reading that runs before and during the work, to show hot work needs a live reading and not one test at the start.

claims.figure: 1,030 workers died from occupational injuries involving a confined space (2011 to 2018); 126 cases of inhalation of a harmful substance; 39 cases of depletion of oxygen
claims.measures: Status: stat. BLS Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries fact sheet, release date 15 July 2020. Annual range: a low of 88 in 2012 to a high of 166 in 2017. Also on the page: 21 drowning cases; tank, bin and vat interiors 205 deaths; ditches, channels, trenches and excavations 203. These are all US deaths inside confined spaces from every cause, not only gas.
claims.source_title: Fatal occupational injuries involving confined spaces
claims.quote: From 2011 to 2018, 1,030 workers died from occupational injuries involving a confined space.
claims.use_in_story: Count up to 1,030 deaths over 8 years, then split off the 126 inhalation and 39 oxygen-depletion cases to show how many were problems with the air.

claims.topic: Hydrogen sulfide deaths 1984 to 1994: co-worker rescuers and what would have prevented them
claims.figure: 80 fatalities from hydrogen sulfide in 57 incidents, with 19 fatalities and 36 injuries among coworkers attempting to rescue fallen workers

claims.topic: Refinery hydrogen sulfide release, 10 October 2024: two dead, 13 taken to medical facilities
claims.figure: Two contract workers died; 13 others were transported to local medical facilities; over 27,000 pounds of toxic hydrogen sulfide gas were released

The CSB update page of 20 November 2024 (https://www.csb.gov/us-chemical-safety-board-releases-investigation-update-into-fatal-hydrogen-sulfide-release-at-pemex-deer-park-refinery-in-deer-park-texas/) lists 'Permit-to-work practices' among nine investigation areas and says two contract workers 'partially opened a flanged connection on piping containing hydrogen sulfide gas'.

claims.topic: Oil and gas safety data: Middle East fatalities in 2024 and its share of hours worked
claims.figure: Middle East 2024: 9 fatalities in 6 fatal incidents, fatal accident rate 0.77; Middle East: 28.2 % of work hours reported by region
claims.measures: Status: stat. IOGP report 2024s, version 1.00, June 2025. Table 26 'Fatalities, fatal incidents, and fatal accident rate by region (2023 - 2024)' (PDF page 56): Middle East fatalities 4 then 9, FAR 0.40 then 0.77, fatal incidents 3 then 6, for 2023 then 2024. All regions sum to the overall 27 and 32 fatalities (FAR 0.82 and 0.77; 17 and 21 incidents). Table 34: Middle East 2024 fatalities 9, of which 2 company and 7 contractor. Appendix A figures 'Percentage of work hours reported by region' (PDF page 110): Middle East 28.2 % in 2024 and 30.6 % in 2023, the largest region both years. FAR is per 100 million hours worked. Totals match a JPT article (32 fatalities in 21 incidents, FAR 0.77: https://jpt.spe.org/report-presents-complex-safety-picture-as-fatalities-rise-but-fatality-rate-dips). Data are from IOGP member companies only. The figures were read from a mirror copy of the IOGP PDF with a local extractor. The IOGP page for the report is https://idms.iogp.org/Documents/1312 (Report 2024s, published 16 Jun 2025).
claims.region: Middle East (IOGP region, includes the Gulf)
claims.publisher: International Association of Oil & Gas Producers (IOGP)
claims.quote: Percentage of work hours reported by region (2024) Middle East: 28.2 %
claims.use_in_story: Zoom a Gulf map and show 9 Middle East deaths in 2024 against 28.2% of the industry's reported hours, to say the region is the largest exposure in oil and gas.

claims.topic: Oil and gas deaths linked to work authorization, confined space and hot work rules
claims.figure: At least 86% of 2024 fatal incidents covered by the IOGP Life-Saving Rules; Work authorization: 17 %, Confined space: 11 %, Hot work: 6 %

The percentages are shares of fatal incidents where a rule was allocated. Counts of fatal incidents in 2024: Work authorization 3, Confined space 2, Hot work 1; 21 fatal incidents in all, 3 with 'Other issue - no applicable rule', so 18 had a rule allocated. Also in the report: 41% of the 2024 fatalities were 'Explosion, fire or burns' (13 fatalities in 5 separate incidents). Global IOGP member data, not Gulf only. Read from the same mirror copy and local extractor as S3-15.

claims.quote: at least 86% of the fatal incidents reported are covered by the IOGP Life-Saving Rules

claims.topic: Lives and cost: OSHA's confined spaces in construction rule
claims.figure: prevent approximately 5.2 fatalities and 780 additional injuries annually; $8.7 million per prevented fatality; $62,000 per prevented injury; monetized benefits of $93.6 million annually
claims.measures: Status: stat (government estimate, not a count of events). Federal Register final rule of 4 May 2015, 80 FR 25365 to 25526. OSHA says an estimated 6 fatalities and 812 injuries occur each year among employees in confined space construction work, and full compliance prevents 96 percent of them. Annual compliance cost is 'between about $59.2 million (when costs are annualized at 3 percent) and $60.3 million (when costs are annualized at 7 percent)'. Net monetized benefit is about $33 million a year at 7 percent. The $8.7 million is OSHA's value of a statistical life, not a bill paid by one firm. The same text is on OSHA's page https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/federalregister/2015-05-04.
claims.source_title: Confined Spaces in Construction, final rule, economic analysis summary
claims.publisher: US Occupational Safety and Health Administration, Department of Labor (Federal Register, 80 FR)
claims.quote: OSHA estimates that the final rule will prevent approximately 5.2 fatalities and 780 additional injuries annually.
claims.use_in_story: Run a cost bar of $60.3 million a year against a $93.6 million benefit bar, with a life icon priced at $8.7 million.

claims.topic: Cost: US structure fires started by hot work, 2017 to 2021
claims.figure: estimated average of 3,396 structure fires involving hot work each year; 19 civilian deaths, 120 civilian injuries and $292 million in direct property damage a year
claims.measures: Status: stat. NFPA Research report 'Structure Fires Caused by Hot Work', September 2023, Key Findings on the first page. The same page says fires where liquids, piping or filters were first ignited were 13 percent of non-home fires and 'accounted for all the civilian deaths that occurred during 2017-2021 in the non-home properties'. Hot work here means welding torches, cutting torches, burners, soldering equipment, tar kettles and power nail guns, so not all fires are gas related. Safety+Health magazine reports the same figures (https://www.safetyandhealthmagazine.com/articles/24698-structure-fires-caused-by-hot-work-new-report-from-nfpa). The PDF came back as binary through WebFetch, so the text was read with a local extractor.
claims.source_title: Structure Fires Caused by Hot Work
claims.publisher: NFPA Research, National Fire Protection Association
claims.quote: estimated average of 3,396 structure fires involving hot work each year from 2017 to 2021
claims.use_in_story: Tick a $292 million a year meter beside 19 deaths and 120 injuries to show what unchecked hot work costs in one country.

gaps: API RP 2009 (hot work), RP 2016 and API 2015 (tank entry) are paid standards. Only the CSB's quote of RP 2009 page 12 and its note that RP 2009 and NFPA 51B recommend written hot work permits were read (S3-09). No API percent LEL or ppm limit for tank entry or hot work was found.

NFPA 51B full text is paywalled. The 1 hour fire watch comes from NFPA committee records, not from the standard's own text (S3-08). The hot work gas limit of 10 percent of LFL was not read inside NFPA 51B. The committee record only says the CSB asked for it and that the committee held it for review with NFPA 326. NFPA's own hot work fact sheet PDF had no extractable text.

No Gulf gas-testing rule beyond Abu Dhabi was read. Dubai Municipality's confined space guideline (DM-HSD-GU39-CSE2) could not be fetched; its URLs returned the portal home page. No Saudi gas-testing limits, no Kuwait, Qatar, Oman or Bahrain rules, and no Gulf national oil company work permit procedures were found. UAE coverage is Abu Dhabi only.

No Gulf hydrogen sulfide or confined space fatality count from a government or peer-reviewed source was found. Gulf evidence is limited to the IOGP Middle East totals (no gas breakdown, member companies only), the Abu Dhabi code and the Saudi high-risk list.
The session's WebSearch budget (200 calls) ran out during this task, so no new sources could be searched for after that point. Later checks used WebFetch on known URLs only.

No cost per gas fatality or per confined-space incident was found. The National Safety Council work injury cost page returned HTTP 403. The cost evidence is OSHA's $8.7 million value per prevented fatality (2015 rule, S3-17) and NFPA's $292 million a year hot work fire loss (S3-18).
The BLS table behind OSHA's '46 worker deaths 2011 to 2017' (S3-11) was not opened. A search summary said 36 of the 46 were in confined spaces. That line is not on OSHA's page, so it is not claimed.
ACGIH's public carbon monoxide page needs a member login. The CO TLV of 25 ppm comes from the ILO/WHO ICSC card (S3-06).

IOGP figures (S3-15, S3-16) were read from a mirror copy of the PDF at ghanaupstream.com, because the IOGP page showed only the description and the PDF text was extracted locally.
